problem_motivation.content: Traditional high-damping alloys suffer from irreversible relaxation processes, poor high-temperature stability, and a trade-off where high damping is mutually exclusive with high strength/ductility.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: However, when exposed to mechanical vibrations and the associated stresses, both crystal defects and interfaces in these conventional alloys tend to rearrange and aggregate. As a result, the whole relaxation process is irreversible and the damping capacity gradually deteriorates ( [1] , [8] ). In addition, these irreversible relaxation processes accelerate when the service temperature increases. This means that structural stability and the high-temperature damping capacity of traditional noise reduction alloys are often insufficient for long-term use ( [8] , [9] ). Moreover, those internal structural features that create high damping ability (mobile defects) scale inversely with mechanisms that lead to good mechanical strength (immobile defects). Therefore, in traditional high-damping alloy design concepts, high damping and high strength/ductility are often mutually exclusive ( [10] ).

prior_approach.content: Snoek relaxation in bcc systems has been used to achieve damping properties.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Snoek relaxation, proposed in 1941 ( [11] ), is suited for equipping materials with damping properties and maintains those over long-term exposure to vibrations. Several bcc (body-centered cubic) systems show Snoek-type damping behavior, where the mechanical energy loss originates from the stress-induced ordering of interstitials ( [12] , [13] ).

prior_approach.content: Conventional Snoek-type damping alloys are the existing baseline for comparison.

prior_limitation.content: Snoek-type high-damping alloys generally lack sufficient strength and ductility for demanding applications.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, these Snoek-type high-damping alloys generally showed insufficient strength and ductility for mechanically highly demanding application scenarios.

prior_limitation.content: Hydrogenated metallic glasses have limitations in size and thermal stability.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: their small dimensions (they are usually produced in small volumes as they require high quenching rates) and low thermal stability make them less suitable for damping applications for larger structures and at elevated temperatures

inspiration_source.content: The current study is analogized to previously reported hydrogen-containing high-damping alloys.
inspiration_source.evidence_span: Similar to the hydrogen-containing high-damping alloys reported previously ( [53] ), the here discussed high interstitial refractory HEAs may be regarded as a kind of high-damping alloys.

causal_claim.content: The addition of oxygen or nitrogen enhances the damping capacity.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The addition of oxygen or nitrogen effectively further enhances the damping capacity

causal_claim.content: High variety of local atomic configurations leads to broad Snoek relaxation peaks.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This effect leads to a Snoek signal in the current HEAs where the relaxation peaks are much broader than a Debye peak.

causal_claim.content: The formation of ordered oxygen complexes is identified as the cause for the enhanced ductility in the O-2 HEA.
causal_claim.evidence_span: ~18.5% of all the oxygen atoms in the O-2 HEA participate in the formation of ordered oxygen complexes, enabling the enhanced ductility of this material

causal_claim.content: The larger atomic size of nitrogen compared to oxygen is the cause for the higher strengthening in the N-2 HEA.
causal_claim.evidence_span: With the addition of 2.0 at % nitrogen, the larger atomic size of nitrogen (atomic radius of 0.75 Å) compared to that of oxygen (0.65 Å) leads to higher strengthening

mechanism_principle.content: Stress-induced position switching of interstitial atoms causes internal friction peaks.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: stress-induced position switch of interstitial atoms gives rise to the corresponding internal friction peaks

mechanism_principle.content: Ordered oxygen complexes are the cause of the additional low-temperature damping peak.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The appearance of an additional low-temperature damping peak in the O-2 material (see Fig. 1B ) also indicates the existence of the ordered oxygen complexes

mechanism_principle.content: The high yield strength of the O-2 HEA is attributed to ordered oxygen complexes providing strain hardening.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: which has been earlier associated with the formation of ordered interstitial complexes that provide high strain hardening

mechanism_principle.content: The high activation temperatures for interstitial reorientation are caused by high atomic-scale distortion fields in the HEA matrix.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Because of the high configuration entropy and severely distorted lattices of HEAs ( [50] ), atomic position switches of interstitials in these matrices are impeded by the high atomic-scale distortion fields ( [51] ).

mechanism_principle.content: The amplitude-independent damping and broadened peaks are caused by the high configurational variety of interstitial relaxation processes.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: However, the high damping capacity of the alloy class discussed here is amplitude independent and originates instead from the high configurational variety of the underlying interstitial relaxation processes characteristic for compositionally complex solid-solution alloys.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors propose that a new class of high-damping alloys combining mechanical strength and high-temperature workability can be realized using Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEAs blended with interstitial atoms.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Here, we report about a previously undiscovered class of high-damping alloys that are both mechanically strong and workable at high temperatures.

evidence_result.content: Activation energy values measured for base, O-2, and N-2 HEAs.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The activation energy H is estimated to be 2.06, 2.40, and 4.06 eV for the reference alloy and the interstitially doped O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively.

evidence_result.content: Yield strength values for the base and doped HEAs.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The interstitial doped HEAs have a strong solid-solution strengthening, i.e., the yield strength was increased to 1138 and 1362 MPa for the O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively.

evidence_result.content: The ductility of the O-2 HEA was observed to double unexpectedly.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Particularly, the ductility of the O-2 HEA was unexpectedly doubled

evidence_result.content: The fitting curves for decomposed relaxation peaks show good agreement with experimental data across all three HEA types.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The fitting curves are in good agreement with the experimental data points, with a correlation index above 0.99.

evidence_result.content: Quantitative measurement of Snoek damping peak heights for the base HEA.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The height of the two Snoek damping peaks is 0.014 and 0.006, respectively.

evidence_result.content: Quantitative measurement of Snoek damping peak heights for the O-2 HEA, including the new low-temperature peak.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The height of the additional peak and of the two high-temperature peaks is 0.005, 0.020, and 0.002, respectively.

evidence_result.content: Quantitative measurement of Snoek damping peak heights for the N-2 HEA.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The peak height of the additional low-temperature peak is 0.002, and that of the two high-temperature peaks is 0.027 and 0.009, respectively.

evidence_result.content: Measured yield strength and damping capacity of the base HEA.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The base HEA exhibits a relatively low yield strength (~810 MPa) and a small damping capacity (~0.014 at 1.0 Hz)

evidence_result.content: Measured yield strength and damping capacity of the O-2 HEA.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The addition of 2.0 at % oxygen enhances not only the yield strength to ~1138 MPa but also the maximum damping ability to ~0.020 at 1.0 Hz.

evidence_result.content: Measured yield strength and damping capacity of the N-2 HEA.
evidence_result.evidence_span: As a result, the N-2 HEA exhibits both improved tensile yield strength (σ y ~ 1362 MPa) and damping properties (tanδ max ~ 0.027 at 1.0 Hz).

constraint.content: The maximum strain amplitude applied during damping measurements was limited to 2 × 10⁻⁴.
The heating rate for damping measurements was constrained to 2 K min⁻¹.
constraint.evidence_span: A heating rate of 2 K min −1

constraint.content: The tensile testing was performed under a specific strain rate of 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
constraint.evidence_span: at the strain rate of 1 × 10 −3 s −1

contradiction.content: Ordered nitrogen complexes were observed, contrary to expectation based on lower frequency of formation compared to oxygen.
contradiction.evidence_span: Unexpectedly, we also observed ordered nitrogen complexes in the N-2 material

contradiction.content: The damping mechanism in these HEAs (amplitude independent) explicitly contrasts with the mechanism in established reference materials (amplitude dependent).
contradiction.evidence_span: One has to note that the main structural features responsible for the high mechanical damping capacity of some of the established high-damping reference materials are highly heterogeneous microstructures, thermoelastic martensite, magnetic domains, or easily moveable dislocations, which generally show an amplitude dependence of damping ( [52] ). However, the high damping capacity of the alloy class discussed here is amplitude independent
